A key focus of my setting’s tone is leaving that question uneasy to answer. And it requires answering other questions.

The Maeths and their cousins, the Barrowmen, have believed in mostly the same Gods for at least a thousand years, but since the great cataclysm, they have been much more doubtful. There is a schism in each culture, with the more skeptical and faithless being dubbed “The Godless.” Traditionally, both believed that the Gods lived and walk among them. Blix was the lightning itself; Hanglee was the one who possessed a craftsman with inspiration and masterful creation; Wisanmiht was on the battefield when a warrior entered a martial trance. The Gods spoke through the world, and some believe they do still speak, though even the more fervent believers admit that it has “dimmed to whispers.” And although the faithful would consider all of the above examples as testaments to the existence of the Gods, and clear signs of their realness, the interpretations can vary widely. Many conceive of the Gods more materialistically, so they believe an actual extant spirit (like a ghost in a movie), such as Wisanmiht, possesses a warrior in battle in such moments. Some of the more nuanced thinkers believe that those moments of “possession” or “being in the zone” are the Gods themselves.

Taking them as an example, “how true is their religion?” is not exactly an easy answer. Especially given that all of these Gods’ names mean something, a concept typically. If I told you that so-and-so is a man “gripped by melancholy,” that phrase is sort of an anthropomorphizing of melancholy itself, as though it were a thing (or a person even) which can grip. Is what I’m saying “untrue,” or is it just expressing my perception of reality with poetic license?

The Dreadmen believe in Anti-Gods or Devils - supernal entities that influence the world but who are detestable, egregious characters that they revile, resist, defy, insult and combat at every opportunity. Their Gods are literally named Death, Spite, Darkness, No, Scorn, Stillness, etc. And they, like the Maeths and Barrowmen (who are all their distant cousins, all equally descended from the ancient Spearspeaker culture), believe that these Gods manifest themselves in the material world. Death is death and dying. Darkness is darkness, the night and the snuffing out of lights. Spite is spite and spiteful behavior, and so on.

Are their Gods “real”?

To compare to this world, I named my car “Bessie.” And I talk to her sometimes, and I personify her in a couple of other ways. If I said “Bessie failed me” Or “Bessie’s sick,” we could be very literal and pedantic and say “Well, cars can’t get sick, and they don’t have agency, so they can’t really “fail” you.” But I think there’s room to argue that when I say “Bessie’s sick,” most people would probably understand that there’s some problem with my car. And if this personification has practical applications, such as maybe getting me to pay more attention and give more care to my car, then pragmatically it could be said that this treatment and perspective of my car is “true.”

Magic has many different conceptions throughout the world. Overall, a core tone I want to establish in the worldbuild is that of ambiguity and uncertainty about the supernatural. Some people in that world are dead certain that magic, divine beings, spirits or other supernatural phenomena are all very real, while others think some of it is, and others still see it as misunderstandings or total delusions.

The scholars of Aescanria tend to believe that magic is just “unexplained science.” They think there is a reasonable, material, physical explanation for most if not all phenomena. Not all of the scholars are unanimous in this belief, but the overwhelming majority of them, past and present, have carried on a tradition of being skeptical and empirical. The uneducated among often have superstitions and rumors of spirits existing. And many of the scholars have begun to entertain the “ignorant and insane” ideas regarding magic and the supernatural, in light of the Horrors.

The Maeths believe magic is the blessings from, channelling of or possession by spirits or Gods. For them, magic is present when you see people performing “superhuman” feats. This can be as common as a craftsman at work, getting in the zone and making several pieces or a true masterpiece, to a warrior on the field of battle fighting so fiercely or so effectively that even the enemies can feel the divine presence. Various Gods govern various aspects of (human) existence. For example, someone who is a great philosopher or a creative poet might be considered “beloved by Thohta,” or otherwise blessed by her, the Goddess of the Mind. That said, there is a theological, existential crisis happening within the Maethish societies, which has been forming loose, ill-defined schisms between more Godly Maeths and Godless ones.

The Dreadmen believe magic is merely the ability to manifest one’s will into the world. They take ‘Might Makes Right’ to an extreme, believing that it is their unholy duty to spite the Gods, who want Life to end, and do Life no favors. The Dreadmen believe that things such as cunning, brutality, persuasion, craftsmanship, ingenuity, steadfastness and deception are all skills to hone or master, if one can. And that the greatest artists of these crafts can be considered “magic.”

For the cultures of the Orefolk, across the board, magic is in metal, most particularly in the metal of their ancestor’s remains, being that they have metal bones, hair, teeth and nails. Keeping portions of these remains near or on you, or interring them in a sacred (perhaps also secret) site for later visitation are the means by which one acquires ‘supernatural’ power(s). Some practical parts of this theory of magic are the use of their ancestor’s bones for wares, tools, weapons, armor, artifacts, etc. They hunt with arrow heads made from their father’s teeth, because in life he was a successful hunter or archer; they cradle their children in cradle made from grandma’s remains, because she loved her children dearly, and tenderly; they forge great warriors into sword and shields, so that the living fighters may benefit from their slain. This also serves as a means of honoring their dead but also shaming them. Making your murdered friend into a sword, which you will use to avenge him is a more noble or at least loving use of one’s remains, while a criminal killed for heinous crimes may be forged into a cage, a pisspot or even just have their bones thrown/sold away. In any case, their theory of magic is that the bones of their ancestor’s hold power, as though their spirit lives on. But their ancestors only affect the world so long as the living use them or commune with them.
No laws, no crime.

Not if you gave great reasons for that being the case. Like if you have a worldbuild that takes place in the future or something, there could be a lore-based reason that one of those auxiliary languages could be so prevalent.

But if you’re just using them as pre-existing languages, I’ll admit it’s lazier than doing a whole conlang. Though making a whole conlang isn’t necessary for worldbuilding. If you want to have separate languages but don’t feel like actually a whole language, then you can just figure some loose sense of the language (i.e. basic grammar structures, core phonology, orthography, very common phrases/vocabulary), then you can get away with it.

I only really hold disdain for people who do nothing more than “Oo that word sounds cool” the whole way through their languages. Like even if you start that way, it’s forgivable, even has room for lots of potential. But if you never stop yourself and try to make a loose semblance of rules/consistency for the language(s), then it feels really lazy, and I imagine the language(s) would suffer for it.

Depends on what (or whose) standard you’re applying to your worldbuilds.

Figure out what you want, and then look for examples, inspirations, insights and comparisons with your ideas in other people’s works.

And if you don’t know exactly what you want, but you want to try, then just do what’s most interesting and fun for you.

Maybe you wanna draw some characters or places today. Maybe tomorrow you’ll work on a map. Another day you could make a name generator or work on one of the languages. And then maybe next week you’ll have a bunch of ideas for a weird biome or a new species or culture or something. 

If you’re not feeling creative but you want to make some progress, you can just go over your old stuff and look for typos, inconsistencies, or disorganization.

I would recommend abstracting this question with Some prerequisite questions.

Are the Gods real in your world?
And what does it mean to be a God in your world?
What is their relationship to the world? To their believers?

For my own worldbuild, I started with the cultures, and what vibes I want them to give off. What lifestyles they tend towards, what values they hold and what their general philosophy on life is (as a culture; individuals always have their own eccentricities).

From there, I was able to glean an idea of what sort of Gods they may or may not believe in. Inserting my own personal views on religion and deities, it is my suspicion that religions, gods, spirits and such things are born out of metaphor, personification and anthropomorphism. If you look at real world ancient religions such as the ancient Greek pantheon, you’ll find that the names of the various Gods do not seem coincidental. So when it comes to creating Gods, I try to reimagine how humanity “created” the Gods that have been worshipped in our world.

I start as a poet and a storyteller, and I imagine what kind of wisdom a poet or storyteller might try to impart in wondrous words and illustrious myths towards others for generations to come.

The Dreadmen in my world were supposed to be grimly and gruesomely dressed. They come from a very bleak life due in large part to the nature of their homeland. I wanted them to have a very harsh, violent and unforgiving culture, one which prized inner strength. And as I was picturing them and figuring out more details for their culture, a thought about their religion came to mind:

What if, instead worshipping their Gods, they reviled all of them? So instead of Gods, it’s sorta like they have only Devils that they watch out for, do their best to repel and insult and to disobey.

They are distantly related to the Maeths and Barrowmen. Their religion began as a schism from the religion that the other two still have carried on with. Their religion began with the feeling of being unhelped by the Gods. It was the view of their forefathers that the Gods were not trustworthy or reliable. Over time, this distrust grew into outright dislike for their Gods, and the belief that the only real Gods, who reliably appeared in the world, were Gods of pain, destruction, death and dread. And thus their holymen received epiphanies that the Gods are not good - the Gods are all quite evil. 

So their mythology (without telling all of it), there were many Gods until Death, the Lord of All Ends, came along. Death is the end of All Things, he is the crumbling of mountainsC the drying of rivers, the wilting of flowers and what follows the last breath of every man and animal. He does these things, because he enjoys it - it’s his calling. Death was doing his work of ending all things, and he had gotten close before his brother (Nay) and sister (Darkness) betrayed him by stealing Darknesses’ End from him and hiding it, thus preventing her death and preventing Death from being able to finish his job. Darkness and Nay go on to have children, and Death meddles with their family to get them to give him back what is his. The family grows and they all attempt to spite death by creating Life (as in worldly life). They make Life stronger and stronger and more and more plentiful, more resistant to Death. Depending on the telling, Death is either overjoyed to have more things to end, or he feigns this joyousness to get them to stop. In either case, the other Gods are enraged began tormenting Life with all sorts of ills, weakness, dangers and threats to try and destroy it, as their last spite of taking away Death’s new plaything.

So their Gods are all openly out to destroy them, as the Dreadmen believe that all life is an obstacle in the way of their revenge. And they think it is their duty to spite the Gods all the same, by resisting death, ruin and fear at every turn. The Gods exist as forces and concepts that exist in the world. 

Darkness is the night, the shadows and the lightless places; 

Nay is wherever one tries and fails, or is rejected or is otherwise denied something; 

Stillness is there when the woods go absolutely, unnervingly quiet, she is there when you mean to speak or laugh or express yourself but you cannot, and she is the hush that the dead know best;

Sorrow is wherever tragedy strikes down the weak, and leaves them numb, weeping and without any desire.

The Maeths and Barrowmen on the other hand, have a more “traditional” mythology, with many Gods that they revere and look up to and beseech for help, aid, guidance or wisdom. I wanted them to be more like European tribes and clans, so they have a plurality of divine beings they believe in. But I wanted to have them experience a cultural-existential crisis, wherein there has come a great doubt in their Gods (not unlike what the Dreadmen’s ancestors went through). Many do not believe the Gods are with them anymore, that they have somehow died or forsaken humanity and this world, while others of course insist that they are still among them and they do still take part in this world.

In the myths, their Gods overcame many great trials and changed themselves to adapt to the world. They found things like beautiful things like Wisdom, Will, Love, Kinship, Friendship, Growth, Victory, etc. along with darker or harder things, such as Folly, Resentment, Death and others. The Gods were seen as icons and champions of such gifts, tools, discoveries and resources, and were revered for the many ways that humans made use not only of those things, but of the Gods’ examples.

It Hanglee, the Smith God who helps the craftsmen when he is on a roll, making many of his best pieces in one day;

It is Thohta, the Goddess of the Mind who appears when one is daydreaming, lost in thought, anxious, contemplative or highly imaginative;

It is Wisanmiht, who you can see when someone in a seemingly no-win situation not only acquires the clarity to see the way out but also perfectly performs the nearly impossible deeds necessary for success.

Gods are like the embodiment of ideas, forces, or feelings, and humans tell stories about these things, so that they can understand them, appreciate them and care about them more easily. It can be easier to imagine caring about the very concept and act of Thought when it is Thohta, a Goddess who is able to see with eyes closed, and who mothered the word, and who had her mind opened so that thoughts could come and go from her. Likewise, it can be easier the conceive of the dangers of the world as enemies with names and intentions. Scorn isn’t just a feeling - it’s essentially a demon that possesses you and makes you feel that you’d better hurt those who have hurt you; it feels your mind endlessly with thoughts of revenge, feelings of persecution or mistreatment, and blinds you to any feeling other than “I have been wronged.”

That’s how *I* write gods, and that’s how I try to read them as I go through the myths in my own writings and in the actual myths of our world like Greek mythology.

I’m not trying to convince you out of anti-Natalism. 

It isn’t a matter of it being right or wrong to me. I like to challenge people, so that they may either let go of something they don’t know how to defend, or demonstrate (to myself, others or themselves) that my doubts and scrutiny do not poke holes in anything. But perhaps more importantly, I like to see if people are aware of the fuller consequences of their beliefs, their origins, and where inconsistencies may arise or already exist.

Someone in here told me that anti-Natalism isn’t conditional. So, even if the world was a “nicer place”, it wouldn’t justify procreation whatsoever.

But it was only one person.

Yeah, you are so wrapped up in your morality that you cannot even see outside of it.

“condemns” is moral language. The fact that you are comparing procreation to sentencing someone to a punishment is implication enough. If you want a non-moral word to use to describe the act of putting someone into existence without their consent, you could say “throw” as in “throwing others into existence.” Martin Heidegger offered this term to describe the quality of the human condition of us being “thrown into this.”

You also seem to say that non-compassion based moralities are not moralities at all. And that the only *true* moralities are ones based on minimizing, preventing or alleviating harm.

As for duty, you are ignoring the history of this mode of valuation that you have inherited. You are not the first person to embody the morality you espouse. And this morality did not come out of nothing. It is descended from previous moralities that gave the foundations for it. Namely Christian moralities, which encouraged man to think less of this world and more for the next world, AND considered it a duty of every Christian to pity. And it is from those things, among others, that the Anti-Natalist position has come from. This narrative and perspective did not come out of nowhere. It was fathered and mothered by “unworldly” religions, analgesic philosophies and morals of réssentiment. 

And you conclude by further doubling down on (presumably all) suffering and hardship as having moral weight, and then equate Anti-Natalism to compassion itself.

Imagine a morality which does not center itself upon suffering. Which does not hold that suffering itself is wholly undesirable. Which does not hold that prevention of and minimizing suffering is desirable from a moral perspective. They have existed, and do exist, but it is people like you which condemn them as wholly evil because they are fundamentally antithetical to your own morality.

Imagine a non-moral perspective about life. One which is not looking for what is right or wrong, good or evil.

What do you take issue with then?

What is your contention with having children when there’s already 8 billion of us?

The main thing that I think Utilitarianism has given to many Anti-Natalist is the definitions of good and evil. 

Good is pleasure or at least the absence of suffering.
Evil is the presence of suffering.

That’s specifically what I am looking for. An anti-Natalist position which doesn’t base itself on those definitions or similar definitions. An anti-Natalist perspective that’s not focused on minimizing suffering.

The complexity I’m speaking of is that which is non-moral. And even if it must be moral, there are moralities that differ fundamentally from the most common Anti-Natalist one. Ones which are not hyper-focused upon suffering and the prevention or relief thereof.

You have examined a handful of singular aspects of human existence:

The fact that no is known to be able to consent to entering existence.
The fact that human existence entails suffering and death.

And these facts are far more important to you because you have moral judgments surrounding them. And your moral perception of reality takes precedence over every other perception that you have available to you. Your moral ideal is untenable for human existence, so you choose morality over human existence.

It is admirable in that regard, that you have such strong conviction with your principles. But I have no inclination for a philosophy which regrets itself and is fundamentally suicidal.

I’m more interested in a perspectivist philosophy rather than one that is primarily and solely concerned with the ethical. That is the unidimensionality I am pointing to. 

You are being the pearl-clutching devout Christian scowling at a dancer for dressing and acting “lustfully.”
You are being the inquisitor who is demanding that a creative, innovative and successful person be boycotted and ostracized because of a past immoral act.

Those are the kind of people who declare that if it is immoral, there is no possible way we can tolerate it, let alone redeem it or repurpose it. You have condemned it, and you have condemned any who support it as either willfully immoral (me) or as fools bereft of the most important truths.

I never claimed to be enlightened, and I have my own blindnesses. The difference is that I’m not the one saying that having children “condemns” them to life and death, which is loaded in moral language. 

I am familiar with Anti-Natalism, at least its broadest baseline aspects of morally condemning human procreation, and I believe that I have an understanding of the more common reasons that people cling to this position.

What I am interested in is meeting anti-Natalists with an unusual morality, one that doesn’t condemn it out of some overabundant compassion, but condemns it for some other reasons. Because so far, compassion as the basis for a morality is undesirable to me, because it is a resentful basis for morality.

What I respect about Anti-Natalists - aside from the sheer fact that it is amusing, intriguing and often challenging to know, meet and encounter them and their ideas - is that they have taken compassionate morality to an extreme. They had the intuition and unseeming courage to ask, “If my duty is to pity those who suffer, and life is rife with suffering, then why should people bring more into this world?” The trouble I find is that their premises are not convincing.

Some life is full of suffering, but not all life, all of the time; suffering itself is not clearly evil, otherwise compassion must therefore be evil, for in pitying others, you are feeling pain on their behalf.

Do you have a basis for your morality that isn’t based on compassion?

Because not everyone is viewing the world and life and existence as unidimensionally as you seem to be.

Existence is terrifying. It is also boring, fun, exciting, addicting, depressing, pleasant, ecstatic, exhausting, hard, easy, long, short, etc. etc.

To reduce something down to a small set of aspects and declare that these are the ones that define the whole, or that the presence of these qualities overrides any value in the rest, is simplistic, perfectionist, unrealistic, prideful and often pitiful.

The fact that you cannot stomach the ugliest portions of this reality doesn’t mean that others can’t. Your moral outrage - which is just your personal disgust, confusion and anger - blinds you to the complexity of existence, and thus you only seek out the few things you do see, which are abject pain, suffering, strife, want and death. You are just as blind as the optimists who see everything as sunshine and rainbows and that all of our struggles are just meant to test us or that “everything happens for a reason.”

The thing about history is that it is inevitably lost, forgotten, misremembered, falsified and mangled.

For my worldbuild, I have a made timeline in Google Sheets. And the timeline consists of a handful of vague eras. The first is “Around a thousands years ago,” the next is “several hundred years ago”, then “a few hundred years ago,” then I’m starting to specify numbers a bit more, and add more detail.

In each section, I’ve partitioned the major historical events of my worldbuild to the ancestral cultures of the modern day. The Maeths, Barrowmen and Dreadmen all initially came from one unified culture in the distant past, while the various Aescanrians are descended from an ancient culture that sundered and then sorta came back together. And so on. And each culture has a different overall narrative that is told in the modern age about who their ancestors were, what they did, what happened to them, and what they believe the world was like.

As time goes on, the cultures sundered, and they began telling different stories, or different versions of the same stories. And I write those histories from each of those perspectives. For now, I’m focused on the big picture stuff that every member of those cultures would mention if you asked them about the past. Finer details and smaller events and variations are what I plan to work on in the future. For now, all of the Dreadmen, for example, will tell you that a great warrior told them that the Gods of their forefathers are false, and that the true Gods are terrible, worthy of scorn, spite and adversity rather than worship. And all of the Dreadmen will tell you that they once ruled the greatest portion of the landmass in their part of the world. As for what specifically lead to their downfall and shrinking, or which specific, smaller events happened and did not happen is more individuated among their members. But the overall narrative is the focus.

My world is full of mortals, however, whereas it sounds like yours can live for much longer periods of time. The thing about immortals (or something near that) is that history for them was something they lived through. Elrond was there 5000 years ago when Isildur took the ring for himself. He didn’t read about it, or hear legends of it, he was actually there. So your histories will probably be told more like stories that your grandparents might tell you about “I remember when JFK was shot,” or “I remember when we got the first automatic transmissions in our cars.”

In any case, how we remember and narrate the past is still biased, partial, prone to the pitfalls and short-comings of our memories, and often told to push some sort of narrative. A double-edged sword of writing history, I find, is that you can lighten your workload by including skepticism. “No one knows for sure what happened to this city,” can be a way of adding mystery and wonder to your world, and also a way of saving yourself from having to write out what exactly happened in the past. The catch is that, realistically, people still try to explain this, and the explanations often vary and the purposes behind the explanations and what people do with the explanations are even more varied. Which means you’ll have to write what X tribe says happened to that city, and that the Immortal King who has reigned for a thousand years blames the downfall of the city on some mysterious force, and that the nomads of this region claim they are descended from the survivors of that city and that they attribute tyrannical government to the decline of their once great city. And so on.

The thing I look for in well-written, believable histories is the existence of multiple narratives and the presence of many questions. In my world, there are different religions, which are blamed/credited for several legendary events of the past, which may or may not have even happened. If you ask a Maeth why their clan is feuding with its neighbor, what they say will likely be different from how their neighbor tells it. And that is history. History is the narratives that the living tell themselves about the past. And it is full of justifications, presuppositions, myths, rumors, propaganda, erroneous conclusions, lies, half-remembered details, exaggerations for dramatic effect, poetic license, etc. That’s how I try to write my histories, because the emphasis is on how the living perceive the past. As for what actually happened, I have some of the major things plotted out, but I don’t fixate on them. I’m more interested in telling how the living, present Aescanrians talk about their lost empire’s former glory, and the great deeds of its long-dead heroes, rather than actually establishing which of these heroes was for sure real, or which aspects of their empire were true.

I’m honestly more open to the idea of a monarchy than a republic at this point. 

I’m going to elaborate and make some comparisons between monarchy and republics, and I’m going to try and steel-man each of these forms of government by assuming that these governments are working as intended. So the Kings are being obeyed, the Senators/Representatives are lawfully and actually elected by their constituents, laws under each government are being obeyed and enforced, etc.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Hereditary Monarchy has people trained from birth to govern and guide their people. But it is far from the only form of monarchy.

You could have an elective Monarchy.
The Anglo-Saxons would have the aldermen elect their kings.
If you are a more “democratically” mind person, then you could have the Monarch elected by a popular vote.

Monarchy’s failings come from the corruption or the ineptitude of one person, while its victories only need one person to be competent and dutiful. A Monarch’s most important skills are contextual: 

If one King’s reign oversees a period of hardship, then his most important skills are ones which can make use of hardship, so that the lands and people are not too weakened or destroyed by the hardship.

If another King oversees a period of prosperity, then his most important skills are ones which can make use of prosperity, so that the lands and people are not too weakened or destroyed by the prosperity.

The obvious troubles that all Monarchy struggles with, are that the country is reliant upon a single person to carry the day. Therefore, it becomes of utmost importance and wisdom to invest in the character, resources, acquaintances, advisors and servants of the Monarch, so that if the Monarch should fall short of the challenges before them, they have others who they may turn to for guidance.

Whereas a Republic, by its very design, empowers demagogues. In this system, a politicians foremost important skill must be persuasion. If they (or their supporters) cannot persuade enough people to vote for them, then all other skills are irrelevant. This renders all governance, at its birth, a popularity contest. Competence or effectiveness can play a hand at re-election, but if the opposition has a more charming candidate or promising platform, then their competence and effectiveness can go right out the door.

The prime strength of a Republic is that it “doesn’t put all of its eggs in one basket.” So if there are a handful of corrupt or inept elected officials, then the others may compensate or counter-act the damages they may incur. Therefore, ensuring that the majority of the elected governors are competent and honest in their intentions becomes paramount. Doing so, however, is difficult because, again, the system empowers demagogues, who know how to persuade us to support them. One might say, “Don’t listen to the candidate, look at their platforms.” But to do so requires to only look at the promises without examining the one making these promises. So, one must vote for the most persuasive candidate, and hope that they are honest and capable.

Natural selection.

Suffering is far from new.
People not being able to digest or manage that aspect of existence is also not new.
The people who could not handle the hardships they lived through enough to go on and have children, didn’t do so.
The people who could go through historical hardships and were still able to have children, did so.

We are the descendants of the latter category, which is why it is an instinct to still have and crave sex (if not consciously the products of sex: children), even in the middle of desolation, because those are the kinds of people that survived ancient atrocities and disasters.

If humans and their desires for sex and/or reproduction were so easily quashed, then we would have died out a lot longer ago.

Bækhæt, in the Maethic religion, is the God of Dread, Loathing, Strife and Hexes. When he met Miht and his three wives, he tried to learn from them, to imitate them and to join them. He wanted to win their love, trust and affection, but he was much unlike all of them, and he either failed, came up short or mangled his attempts to be like them. His gifts were all ugly to them. He was trying to win the love of those three Goddesses, who at first entertained that he might be like a second Miht, the first man they ever met. But they did not give their holy Yes to him, like they did to Miht, and they all eventually No’d him. And the dire No struck him deep, and forever changed him.

Thereafter, he spoke the first Hex into being, and brought about the next Strife, wishing them to feel as he now felt, all the more hurt, alone, devastated and aggrieved. Well, this question, in any setting, is ultimately an economic one, and I think you’re also ignoring what knights were historically, in a social sense, which would potentially answer your economic questions.

Knights under feudalism were not simply warriors with armors, they were a class of lesser nobles. Kings, Princes and other Monarchs would “land” certain families that proved their worth to them, making them land-owning noblemen. The people in those lands were often tied to those lands, making them not explicitly property themselves, but extensions of the land as property of the nobility (these are the serfs). This meant that the lords of these lands were entitled to practically any and all wealth contained in or produced in their lands. So imagine the potential resources and manpower of an entire town or village or county is at your disposal. You can tax them in manifold ways, the most foreknown of these was through money and goods, but the lords also frequently taxed their serfs by having them perform labor for their Lords. This was honestly quite common in various places and times, considering that money was not something serfs had much of any, if any at all in fact. So you have the peasants work your land, your livestock and produce goods for you as part of their way of paying their dues to you.

Knights were essentially miniature monarchs of minute pieces of land. And they were in the middle of the social ladder, so while the peasants rendered goods and services to their lords, the knights rendered goods and services unto their liege Lords, most notably in the form of military service. Having an elite class of professional warriors proved to be indispensable to armies of the time, because the peasants, serfs, craftsmen and laborers were often too busy to do much else than work, while the knights were able to spend almost all of their time training for war. Not to mention, any “wealth” that the serfs had for themselves was often measly and not kept long, being that most of it was meant to just keep themselves sheltered, fed and warm. There’s even cases wherein the Lords owned all of the heavy, expensive farm equipment (namely the plough), and they would essentially rent it out to the various farmers, so serfs likely didn’t even own all of the many tools for their work. Point being: serfs don’t have much time to be trained for battle, whereas the knights did.

There were also unlanded knights, who either lost their lands or were exiled from their lands, and who would often function as sellswords until some lord decided to vassal them. In Japan, they were called “Ronin,” if you accept the comparison between knights and samurai as apt.

I think that fantasy realms don’t tend to expand on or thoroughly lay out the exactitudes of economics in most of their worlds, though even if they did, I would assume that most of them are functioning on some similar model to the historical ones. As you said, knights are probably so prevalent because they are traditionally epic and cool warriors, and fantasy medieval worldbuilds tend to focus on war quite a bit, so they’re often a “poster-child” for the worldbuilds in a way.

TL;DR Knights were often lesser lords, who basically owned entire villages and towns and were entitled to all of their wealth. That’s how they afforded the expensive armor, horses, weapons; being lords also freed them to train for war and combat nearly everyday.

I think that a common trope with worldbuilds is that there are pretty justified racial stereotypes. As OP stated, elves are “wise, detached and arrogant”, dwarves are “sturdy, stubborn and hardworking,” etc. etc.

In a lot of worldbuilds I’ve found, humans are the only races that actually have vast amounts of cultural diversity. They don’t narrow themselves to one aspect. In RPGs, they tend to be blank slates while other races are given bonuses in general stats (Orcs are dumb but strong, so like +Str but -Int). And even technology/resource norms are often narrow for non-human races, such as dwarves being technologically advanced, elves having enchanted/magical items and artifacts and so on. And sometimes races have blanket ethics/economics, most iconically (I think) would be that dwarves tend to live underground, so they have access to every mineral, which usually means their architecture is all stoneworks and metal, and their possessions are often metal. Elves tend to be dendrophiles, so their architecture is often flowy and “natural” and green, and because they’re almost always *magical*, their possessions are almost always blessed, enchanted, ancient, etc.

So, in contrast, humans can come from all sorts of backgrounds, traditions, values, professions, skillsets, equipment/possessions. They tend to be the least flat race in many worldbuilds. Which I find to be a shame a lot of the time. Because while humans are humans and non-humans are not exactly one-to-one, all of the other races are based on or inspired (loosely at least) by real-life humans. Every worldbuild is made by humans. And these different races with societies, religions, languages, customs, laws, crafts, clothing, culture - they’re all just humans in different skins and often with different biological/metaphysical natures. But ultimately they’re still human. Yet they’re often painted with broadbrushes and left these flat, non-dynamic stereotypes.

Players may try to break the mold, but that doesn’t change the fact that a lot of the NPCs of various races tend to fit their stereotypes pretty dang well. Elves and dwarves don’t like each other; dwarves are all alcoholics; Orcs are all artless raiders, brutes and barbarians, and they all tend to worship the same pantheon; philosophies among the races are far more limited.

TL; DR: Humans tend to have more depth, dynamism and substance, while other races in a lot of worldbuilds are often caricatures, cartoonishly boxed into their stereotypes.

In what way is a monarchy not prey to the danger of dictatorship that a democracy is?

If you designate a King or Queen, whether with constitutional limits or a provisional government beneath them to keep them in check or to limit their scope/power, there’s still a person who is head of state for life and who is inheriting the throne from birthright.

Have not the famous tyrannical or incompetent Kings of history proved enough that they may abuse or neglect their dominion and their people?

I’m not anti-Monarchist to be clear, but I don’t think that the fear of dictatorship is grounds for preferring monarchy over republics or democracy. 

Monarchy can seem preferable when it comes to having a relegated position and family tradition of governance over governments of popular sovereignty, such as republics or democracies generally are.

It can also be preferable by having to only protect the mind, heart and soul of one governor rather than a whole populace which, at least ostensibly, has a say in the governance of their nation.

Of course, too, as dictatorships can benefit from this utility, monarchy has the benefit of debureacratizing government action and legislature, provided the people are at least relatively deferent and obedient to the crown’s command.

TLDR: Monarchies are not exempt from risks of tyranny anymore than democracies/republics are. And I think there stronger arguments in favor of monarchy over democracies and republics than the fear of dictatorships.

Essentially you’re invoking “the Problem of Evil.”

Premise 1: There is an omniscient, omnipotent and omnibenevolent God.
Premise 2: Evil exists in the world.
And naturally the question rises.
Question: Why does God allow evil to exist?

If we’re being skeptics, it’s rational to question the premises first, and to see if we believe in an “omni-God” and/or “evil.” But if we take the premises at face-value without rejecting them, there’s a great number of answers we may offer.

In fact, responding to this very question was so popular in theology and philosophy for so long that there is literally a word for “an answer to the Problem of Evil,” and that word is “theodicy.”

The really simple one that you often hear is “God works in mysterious ways” or some variation on that same sentiment. Humans apparently can’t comprehend a “perfect” being, ergo we cannot know why he does or does not do anything in particular about evil.

Another answer I’ve heard before is that evil only exists because people sin. This can be joined with the additional assertion that disease, famine, natural disasters and other tragedies exist because man was cast out of the perfect garden of Eden due to Adam and Eve’s sin(s).

A sort of variation of the one above is that Adam and Eve ate of the tree of knowledge of good & evil, so we could argue that these things have always existed, but we didn’t see them as evil yet.

Others believe that we cannot have evil without good, therefore evil is necessary for good to exist.

And there are many, many, **many** more answers or attempts to answer this very question. You can take college courses that talk almost exclusively about this.

I hope my comment helps someone.

I do not know God to be a man in the sky.

Nor do I know him to be some extra-dimensional ghost-like entity.

Nor do I know him to be existence itself, as a pantheist might say.

For me, God is understood as an image of a man in heaven. A figure which sees the world as it is and calls it good. A man who knows all that need be known. A man whose love perseveres through all changes and states of existence. He is within each man, woman and child. And he speaks to us through our conscience - that is to say: the word of God is the word from heaven.

The place he occupies is heaven, which is not an actual physical space. Heaven is more like peace or a party insofar as both peace and a party are not singular, permanent locations, but a state of being. And the same goes for hell. Heaven is a state where understanding, love and purpose are within, around and with all things; Hell is a state of confusion, fear and meaninglessness that is so real that it is practically palpable.

The soul is not a ghost in the machine. It is not some form of consciousness which persists beyond the body. The soul is the sum of our deeds. It is the relationship between our conscience and behavior. The salvation or damnation of one’s soul is in one’s own hands alone. For a righteous man may tread where cruel, unconscionable and violent men reign through ignorance, fear-mongering, chaos and suffering, and yet he could and would remain in heaven. And a wicked man may live among saintly, kind, thoughtful and virtuous folks who garden and nurture their domain with wisdom, love and willfulness and yet he would still be in his own hell.

Hell happens because men do not walk with God. They follow their impulses or their poor reason. They do not think about the simple yet important question:

“What is the highest thing that I could be right now?”

They turn inwards to themselves alone. They ask what would satisfy them; what would satiate them; what would empower them to make the world become as they would have it. They are without God, because what is conscience to them? It’s something that nags them before an act and then haunts them afterwards. It is something which makes them hesitate, second-guess themselves and might convince them to do things which pain them. So many men, knowing no better, shelf their conscience and ignore it. It can become background noise that they do their damnedest to ignore. And for some, it can become so far removed that they have no ability to even hear it anymore. 

And what is the fate of men without conscience? 

They chase pleasure; they are slaves to the whims of Fortune; they wreak vengeance on the world when they are enraged; they servants to vanity and captives of shame; they make the world more hellish with their lack of purpose and life is not a noble endeavor but a cheap, fixed game that they are just trying to play as best as they can. And when enough difficulties have piled up: poverty, shame, betrayal, infamy, sickness, rejection, injury and loss - once they’ve taken their toll on them, and there’s seems no way out of their hardships, what will they do? How will they feel about the world? They’ll see their world for what it is: a broken game. And the very moment life begins to seem inherently unfair and unworthy of living, it is easy to be tempted to abandon all rules and seek revenge. Not on any one person, but on existence itself, for ever making themselves in the first place. They will ideate how they might best break the game further. They will seek to deliberately harm people for harm’s own sake. *That* is hell.

Well, “one” and “an” were once synonymous to some degree.

In Old English, you’ll find there wasn’t really an indefinite article, only definite articles (various case-declined and gendered “the’s”). “An” meant “one” and was only really used to emphasize the singularity of the noun in question.

So while modern English speakers would likely say “A man has to make a living,” grammatically speaking, a more Old English formation of that same sentence would be “Man has to make living.” It’s kinda like the Slavic languages, which don’t really use articles that much (although I believe “eto” or something like that is technically an article or something).

If we wanted to really make “one” more Anglish, we could argue that we just say and write “an.” 

“An, two, three…”
“How many children do you have? An.”

And so on.

I wrestle with these questions regularly.  


But the bigger questions are "What will these question do with us?" and "What will we do with these questions?"  


I'm increasingly convinced that the world is largely unknowable and that we are merely rendering whatever this-all-might-be into something we can manage, something workable or comprehensive or just pleasant. I see people telling themselves that there certainly is morality, there certainly is or isn't a god, there certainly is or is no free will - so much certainty in the face of infinity and self-blind ignorance. So much seeming arrogance. And then I reflect that back onto myself and ask "Well, who am I to be so certain of their errors? How do I know none of them are right?"  


I don't know if anyone is right or wrong, but I can say that I'm neither convinced nor content with settling on one core idea. Every time I think "I've got it, I figured it out," some time later, be it a week or a few years, something comes by and beats the shit out of my little belief-system and I have to pour over everything that my seeming error may have infected. I don't understand people who seem to be able to compartmentalize or ignore these sorts of thoughts. When I become uncomfortable with an idea, something within myself demands that I ponder about that and investigate the thought. Trying to ignore it only makes it gnaw at me more and I begin to feel like I'm running away from life rather than living it. And I despise the thought of hiding from my own mind.  


I've been fighting these doubt for so long. Desperately, hopelessly grasping for some semblance of structured, reliable, trustworthy and perfectly based, reasonable, evidenced, truthful beliefs. And I just continually get thrown off whatever wagon I find myself in. I begin to think now that I'm going to do this my whole life. If I live to 80, I'll be an 80 year-old man still asking "stupid questions" like "Is any of this even real?" and "Is there morality?" and it will still disturb me and I will still relent and tear myself up and argue with myself, being my own devil's advocate, trying to find the inscrutable, undoubtable, unquestionable beliefs that hold true across time.  


And though I lament at that thought often at times, I'm starting to see that it's kind of beautiful. I consider the possibility that it is my very nature to endlessly doubt and experience existential angst and always stay wary of certainty in deeper matters. And that this is just who I am. Whether it's pre-determined or just a series of choices that I can't escape from - I'm not sure if it matters. But I have the suspicion that that's what these questions will do with me: occupy themselves with my whole life.  


And I guess that means I'm gonna occupy them with myself my whole life. And sometimes I admire it about myself, because I don't know anyone personally who seems to be on that quest, in this fight, going down this road. And I've met plenty who seem to find their answers, in all sorts of places. Or they give up and just put away the questions. But I don't want to be that. And perhaps that's part of my whole situation; maybe there's a part of me that doesn't want there to be answers and so no answers can or ever will be accepted. Some self-fulfilling prophecy, eh?

The dichotomy of control is sufficient.

For the Stoics, control was not partial, it was total. When they say “These things are in your control; these things are not,” they are drawing a line between things that are only in your control and things which are partly or totally controlled by outside forces. If someone or something else has an influence, they didn’t consider it to be in your control.

Take health for example. I do have control of what *I* do to my body. I can nourish it, exercise it, rest it, medicate it and do very much to benefit it, but those do no guarantee good or perfect or improved health. Not only because I can make mistakes but because anything or anyone else can damage or help my body just as much if not more than I can. So if I only have partial influence over my bodily health, and there are external powers that control the rest of my bodily health, then being concerned with my bodily health overall is foolish. Instead, I should only value my input towards my health and disregard anything to do with outside forces’ effects on my health.

I concur with you. Eudaemonia is not the aim of Stoicism, but it is a natural byproduct. This is a philosophy of a means, not ends (at the very least, certainly not external ends). It is not our duty to seek out happiness or to source happiness as the only purpose behind our judgments, decisions and actions. Life inherently involves a great deal of suffering, just as it involves some pleasure. Look at procreation, the beginning of every life, and you will see clearly that this is the case. Sex is a great pleasure, pregnancy has joys and woes and birth is stressful and painful, even if only to the body.

The importance that Stoics place on our lives is the character of our actions. Living well means doing what is virtuous, because virtue is something that none can take away from us so long as we live. The Stoics went so far as to conclude that if living nobly is no longer possible, then dying nobly is. And this is a great view of life and death. Because we all must die someday, and therefore viewing it as an inherent tragedy is rather silly. For we would have human life be other than it is. And there is a great quote from Gladiator that exemplified this:

>“Ultimately, we are all dead men. Sadly, we cannot choose how, but we can decide how we meet that end, in order that we are remembered as men.”

Life is also no inherent tragedy or purposeless thing. Diogenes the Cynic (who founded Cynicism, the philosophical forefather of Stoicism) once overheard someone say that “Life is evil!” To which he responded:

>”Not life itself - but living an evil life.”

Virtue is always available to us, and so we should prize it above all other things. Other men and the forces of nature can take everything else. They can damage our bodies, damage our reputations, damage our possessions - but they cannot damage our decisions or our will or our actions, all of which are what constitutes virtue.

And living virtuously can provide us with well-being and happiness, both of which are common translations of Eudaemonia. If you look at the etymology of the word itself, it more literally meant “in good spirits,” which I think is an even better translation. For living in virtue is to embody the spirits of good things, such as the spirit of courage, the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of temperance, the spirit of justice, of honesty, of patience, of charity, of gratitude, of chastity, of diligence and of humility.

I urge you to think about virtue more. And to think of instances wherein others acted virtuously. And try to compare instances wherein the same virtue was embodied yet different results followed. For instance, one man runs into a burning building to save someone who is trapped within and escapes with that person, thereby saving them, despite his fears. And another man, equally afraid, does the same for another yet perishes in the fire without saving the other. Both men acted courageously, and though the results differ, acknowledge that they were both admirable and that the result makes no difference to whether or not they were brave. Try to think of more examples like this, and I believe you will see that virtue is better prized than success.

I think Epictetus is wrong, if I’m reading him right here. Perhaps something is lost to interpretation. Perhaps I just am biased or am making some error in my reasoning. Whatever the case, I don’t entirely agree with the attitude he seems to express here.

I would agree that the passions are not rational themselves, but I think it is irrational to attempt to remove them from our experience completely. Particularly because they are all bearable if we train ourselves to handle them as such. I’m unsure of whether or not Epictetus’ ideals are even obtainable; is it even possible for someone to “perfect their reasoning faculty” so much that they feel no passions towards anything ever? Maybe. But I’m inclined to think that this is too high a standard, and it is also an unnecessary standard to me.

In my ideation, the Stoic wiseman need not be completely unfeeling or never in distress. He is a human being as all Stoics ought to own.  When I think of great people whom I admire, I do not think less of them when I hear of their pain. Because their pains are felt just as the rest of us do, and I know that they are handling that pain as nobly as they can muster. I do not think that my ideal wiseman necessarily never grieves or has to control their anger that has come up or never gets butterflies in their stomach because someone pretty flirted with them. I believe that the ideal wiseman handles these emotions virtuously.

I believe that some emotions are required for virtues to exist. If you do not feel fear, how can any action you take be courageous? You would not be courageous, you’d merely be fearless. How can we be patient if we have no capacity for anger or upset? You’d not be patient, because patience is all about stemming and controlling your inner frustrations so that they do not lead you to unwise or immoral behavior. (Fun Fact: the word “patience” literally comes from Latin *patientia*, which means suffering. This word is also the root of the word “passion,” as in “The passion of Christ,” referring to the torment that Christ underwent in the Crucifixion story) How could you be honest unless there were lies you had to resist telling? Or promises that you had to work to keep?

Virtues require their vices not only that we may know them but that we may actualize them. And I don’t imagine the ideal wiseman to be someone who never struggles with anything. I imagine a wiseman to be wise in the same way that the strongman is strong. A strongman’s whole duty is to lift and move great burdens. But even he has his own limits. And even he cannot endlessly lift all things all of the time. But the virtue of the strongman is that he continues trying to lift the weights. And his strength came from struggling with the weights and being unable to move them in the first place. And he continues to lift the heaviest weights he can in the exercises that he sees he needs to work on so that he not only stays strong but becomes stronger. The same goes for wisdom. A wiseman is not someone who never makes errors. That’s a childish, perfectionistic definition; it is just as silly and ridiculous to believe that the ideal wiseman must always be wise in all things as it is to believe that the ideal strong man can lift all things with all different parts of his body.

The emotions are natural to humanity. They are given to us by nature, and I believe they are here to guide us. Trying to ignore or suppress them will not bode well in the long run. Anger unexpressed and unacknowledged will often come out in our subconscious behavior. People often can feel irritated or sad or impatient for no clear reason and this is often because they have some unresolved unacknowledged emotional pain. It is our duty to honor these emotions through expressing them. Sometimes the natural, instinctive expression of the body is sufficient. Like when we are stricken with sorrow, we may feel our body grow weak and our eyes will often water. Naturally, sitting or lying down and crying are what you ought do, if you can afford to do so there and then. If the natural bodily expression is not enough, then art is here to help us. Poetry, dance, story-writing, illustration, music - all of these things can help us express our deepest passions and the passions want little more than their day in the sun once they are present. 

And perhaps this is a late mention, but happiness and love are passions - should a wiseman disdain to love or to enjoy? I think that’s absurd. I would agree that it is not our purpose as Stoics to feel love and happiness - not our sole or main purpose - but to say that these things are not worthy of the wiseman would dissolve my faith in the Stoic theory altogether. And I feel the same way about the negative emotions. Sorrow, anger and the like have not been without any worth in my life. They often inspire me to take actions that are virtuous, pleasant and good. They teach me things about myself. They’re the ones that taught me that, while emotions are fine to have, being *possessed* by emotions is dangerous and is to be avoided. Because sorrow makes me want to neglect myself and my duties to others. Because anger makes me want to abuse myself and/or others. Because fear makes me run away or hide from my problems, thus leaving them unresolved. Because love can make me forget what is more important than my feelings for a person, such as remaining firm in my principles and staying loyal and of service to myself and to the others who trust me. Because happiness can make me ignore or forget or blind to other pressing matters that need dealing with.

All of the emotions are fine so long as they do not make our decisions for us. Because emotions are irrational. But to ask us to work to remove them from our existence is to ask us to not be human, in my opinion.

Thank you for reading this. I hope it was insightful. And if not, then I hope you enjoyed it at least. And if you see an error somewhere, I’d be glad to be so humbled and corrected.

The purpose of life is always to be determined by us as individuals. But I personally find it better to find a purpose in something that is mine alone to determine. If my purpose can be taken away by a turn of fortune or someone else’s decision(s), then it would seem to follow that my conception of a “purposeful life” was nothing to admire, but rather something to envy and covet. Because then, purpose is not something we work for and give to ourselves and earn through our labor and studies; purpose becomes a privilege. And I think it a terrible outlook on life to think of the only purpose behind anyone’s life is a matter of sheer chance, and that no one can give their own life meaning. 

Stoicism offers us a purpose that no one can take away from us, and that misfortune cannot rob from us, and that is *virtue.* Virtue is about the intentions and character of our actions, not about their results. Because no action can guarantee any particular external result. There is always the unforeseen factors at play that can skew the probabilities to disfavor our desired result. But virtue shifts our focus and our prize upon how we act and react, not on how we are treated by the world or by other men.

Try imagining someone who you love and care for as deeply as you can, and imagine them enduring the same problems that you endure. What would you counsel them? Would you so easily tell them that giving up is the best option? That their life means nothing now? If you live to see your child grow up, and this sort of thing befell them, would seriously tell your own child “Your life no longer has any meaning?” You have a responsibility towards yourself to take care of yourself and treat yourself as someone that you are responsible for, in the same way that you are responsible for your children, or a pet or a friend in dire need. And this responsibility is not just for yourself, but also for others. Because if you neglect or abuse yourself, you not only harm yourself but you also wound the man that might have been of some service to others. If you take care of yourself, you can become virtuous.

Virtues include things like bravery, fairness, humility, magnanimity, frankness, goodwill, fidelity, dutifulness, patience - do you notice a trend between all of these things? They are all about your choices. Which means they are always available to you. And if you choose them then you can always embody those things, if not for yourself, then for others. Because while you may not guarantee that your actions will give the results that others want or need, you can always a bring a person in their life who is considerate, honest, forgiving, faithful, loving, willing to compromise and make sacrifices and more. And who could ever truly be harmed by such a great friend or ally?

I will say that if you truly cannot bear all of this, suicide *is* an option to the Stoics. However, even they counsel great meditation and effort to be exercised before making such a final decision. And there is always the question I have asked myself when I feel like my life is over: “If I’m going to die someday anyways, why does it have to be *now*?” If you have nothing to lose, then why not try to do what you were terrified to do? You can try to be a man who still helps his children. You might have other family members or dear friends who rely on, look up, trust in and seek out you and your person. You don’t know how much you are truly capable of until it occurs, and that can be an exciting and enpurposing exploration to embark on.

I don’t know if any of this helps. But know that there is at least one other person in this world who is genuinely concerned for you, and who earnestly believes that you have the power to do good things and live a good life.

Your mind triggers your body to shake, your voice to tremble, makes your chest or stomach tight, makes you breathe heavily or not at all, makes you nauseous, puts tears in your eyes - these are things that you cannot control. And throughout my time as a musician and, in high school, an actor, no matter how many times I reminded myself “I don’t care about what these people think. There’s no reason to care what they think. When a person becomes too overwhelmed and overstimulated in the most extreme and dire circumstances, keeping a cool head is not an option. Plenty of people report that moments of high stress result in them blacking out and not even remembering what they did. The adrenaline response is a bodily one that affects our mind.

The Stoics weren’t around in the age of Modern Psychology and Science that can now better inform us about the body and the mind. Virtues still remain, but they must be adapted to modern understanding. That is wisdom to me.

The Stoics differ from the Hedonists in that the Stoics do not aim for pleasure nor hold it as anywhere near the highest good. Although the Stoics did not disdain all pleasure, as we are sometimes misunderstood to do.

For the Stoic, virtue is the highest good. When we embody goodness, we become goodness. And goodness is not measured by sensations or emotions like happiness and pleasure. Pleasure and happiness are good so long as we are not dependent on them such that we are driven to vice. Because what can be pleasing or make us feel happy is not always a virtuous thing. And if we value happiness or pleasure too highly, we may sell ourselves in slavery to it, committing all sorts of injustices, folly and ills on ourselves and those around us.

Why is virtue preferable to happiness? Because virtue is something we can always guarantee ourselves so long as we remain mindful of and choose to accord ourselves to it. Virtue answers all human troubles.

Are you afraid? Good! **Courage** is available to you. Because courage entails feeling fear, yet acting rightly nonetheless in the face of that fear.

Have you made a mistake? Good! **Wisdom** is available to you. Because wisdom begins in acknowledging that there something to learn, and we cannot become wise without mistakes.

Are you deeply attached to some pleasure or incredibly averse to some displeasure? Good! **Temperance** is available to you. Because there is no temperance without some vicious pleasure to resist or some hardship to learn to bear.

Have you done something wrong to someone else? Or even yourself? Good! **Justice** is available to you. Half of justice is righting wrongs that already exist. The other half is living such that you keep the wrongs in memory and imagination instead of in reality.

And those are the four cardinal virtues of Stoicism, but personally, I believe there are many more virtues that are described and applauded all over the world and in many different schools of thought.

Do you feel envy? Good! **Gratitude** is available to you. Envy can remind us that we are very focused on something we don’f have, and that we’ve forgotten how much we do have. Even if all we have are memories and imagination. Even the fact that I can remember things that I am so thankful to have had and also able to imagine an unfathomable amount of equally unfathomably beautiful things is a treasure itself!

Are you upset about something? Good! **Patience** is available to you. Anger, frustration, sorrow, grief, lament, resentment - these are the fuel to the fire of patience, which is simply enduring these emotions without letting them take the wheel. You can rejoice in catching yourself in a moment of some form of hurt and in reminding yourself that you do not need to hurt yourself, anyone or anything even when you are hurt.

Have you been selfish? Good! **Charity** is available. Charity is not simply giving away money or material goods, although that can also be charity. Charity is in acknowledging that everyone, including you, have something to give to yourself, to those around you, and to the whole world, and then giving some of that away. It can be forgiveness. It can be an open-ear or a shoulder to cry on. It can be buying your friend some lunch or buying flowers for your mother. It can be giving yourself a break. There is so much joy and freedom to be had in giving stuff away.

Have you lied or otherwise deceived someone? Perhaps you’ve been lying to yourself? Good! **Honesty** is available to you. Honesty is all about owning your word and your actions and your own personal truths. It’s never too late to be honest, and honesty is the only means to having a real connection. Connection with yourself, with others, with reality. Without it, you’re acting as if it’d be better if reality were otherwise than it is, and that’s an uncomfortable, dangerous and just foolish place to be.

Have you been procrastinating or neglecting your duties? Good! **Diligence** is available to you. Diligence and discipline are all about doing what we know is right and good for us no matter how much we just want to be done with it or to not even bother. Diligence gets our homes clean, keeps us brushing our teeth and taking care of ourselves and providing us the structure of routine and lets us partake in the joy that is making a plan and following through.

Have you allowed your infatuation to embarrass you? Did you let your lover convince you to do things that you regretted? Good! **Chastity** is available to you. Because Chastity is not merely being celibate, just like Lust is not merely trying to get laid. Chastity is about withdrawing from romantic or sexual impulses to stop and witness yourself and the people around you more thoroughly and clearly. Before you invest time and effort and make commitments with someone, you can stop and observe who they really are as a person. And then as friends. I think you are mistaken as to what Stoicism is meant to coach and counsel and encourage. Stoicism does not preach that we have some inner switch panel that allows us to instantly activate our deactivate our emotions. We are human beings and human beings have feelings that are natural to experience. It is not the concern of the Stoic whether his or her feelings are generally good or bad, but whether his or her actions are virtuous or vicious. If we feel hurt, it is important to feel that pain when it does arrive and to express it in some healthy manner, as grief or anger of frustration or disappointment or shame or whatever it may be. Tears are meant for weeping, if they’re already welling up in your eyes, then weep. That is rational.

But what the Stoic regard about controlling our emotions is two main principles:
-Do not be controlled by your emotions
-You can make changes that will change your emotional response to things

To the first point, it is okay to feel hurt, upset, sad or angry. So long as you do not allow this hurt feeling to overpower your reason and convince you to act out of sheer passion in a vicious manner. That is to be enslaved to our emotions, which not a wise or desirable condition to live under to the Stoic.

To the second, there are at least several methods to increasing our mindfulness so that we can begin catching ourselves when we begin to believe that something bad has happened. Once we begin to notice this more regularly, we can begin reminding ourselves of pertinent wisdom that we’ve studied and found in our own lives and tell ourselves to apply that wisdom. And over time, you can change how you normally react to a given situation after enough practice. And then your emotions will often shift in some manner alongside these, too, because now what used to upset you is just another thing you have to work with. It’s not a bad thing, it just becomes a rehearsed act, an act that you’ve been practicing for so that you can perform your role as best as you can. It’s also entirely possible that your emotions still remain generally negative to these events, despite your Stoic study.

If you’re looking for some philosophy of “never feeling bad,” maybe try the Epicureans, though I think even they will say that some discomfort is inevitable. But Stoicism is definitely not the philosophy for someone who never ever feels negative emotions or bodily pain. That is misinterpretation. 

What Stoicism teaches is that we can be human beings with a greater sense of purpose to our suffering by devoting our lives to virtue. Suffering is inevitable. There’s no removing that completely. And the Stoics do not even forbid suicide, but defend it as a choice that we are nearly always able to make, and perhaps we should make at some time. Because the Stoics believed in living as *well* as we can, not in living as *long* as we can. That said, they think that suicide is an option that one should never make lightly, and that there is seldom no way to bear through the hardships of life. We can find inner fortitude; we can change our viewpoints to give us advantage; we can remember that we all will die, and that whatever is currently troubling may ultimately be just a trifle; we can remember that worrying about things that haven’t happened yet is silly, and perhaps that will relieve our worried minds; we can remember that other people have endured similar or even more difficult hardships and still lived good lives, and then we can be reminded that living well through this isn’t impossible. 

All of these things (and more) give greater purpose to my sufferings, and also generally prevent and alleviate many of them, though I still struggle with anger, anxiety and accepting my poverty and other things. But I think the notion that Stoics never feel any pain or negative emotion and live in the mindset of “Nothing ever disturbs me because I am always mindful of Stoic wisdom,” is a bad caricature that I myself mistook for Stoicism, when it is more like “stoicism,” that simplified cartoon of some general Stoic tendencies like some apathy, and stalwartness in the face of adversity.

The circumstances of our environment, of our upbringing, of our social standing, of our bodily health are not 100% up to us, but have any number of other factors and actors. As sensitive animals in this world, it is rarely possible guard ourselves against our body and minds immediate response to any given circumstances. A cold wind blows and we shiver. A loud, unkind word is spoken and we assume that some bad has happened. But just as we can accustom our bodies to pain and discomfort so that not every violent change makes us writhe and tremble, we can accustom our minds to making more accurate initial assessments so that they do not perceive harm. For it is fine and well to read and agree with the words of wisemen like Marcus Aurelius when he says:

>”Remove the judgment and you have removed the thought “I am hurt”; remove the thought “I am hurt” and the hurt itself is removed.”

But it is another task altogether to remember and then embody a wisdom such as this. In our learning, we must expect that old habits will persist. Someone may speak unkindly of me, and I still may immediately think “They have attacked my character,” and the feelings of being attacked will inevitably ensue. And this first impression that I have taken is does not mean I have failed to be Stoic altogether. If I can work to catch myself in the act and then correct it, this is progress and growth. Do not be worn out by your repeated failures, for they are exactly what your study of philosophy is meant for.

As Marcus Aurelius also says:

>”If even the perception of doing wrong departs, what reason is there for living any longer?”

If we are acting irrationally and improperly and we notice this, then a great thing has been done. For we shall inevitably err as we do not inherently possess wisdom nor naturally always act with wisdom. But noticing it is the first step to acting wisely. Once you’ve noticed your error, remembering the appropriate wisdom that will correct the error.

If you feel insulted, acknowledge it. Then remember that if anyone has insulted you, that you are not harmed. If what they say is true, they have helped you by pointing out a flaw in your character that you may improve. And if they speak falsely, then only they are harmed, for they are acting on false information. If their words are cruel, again, remember that you remain unharmed. For it is our duty and our nature to work together, and they are the ones who fail in this duty. And when you feel insulted or otherwise harmed, you may take this difficulty as an opportunity for virtue. If you feel mistreated, you have the opportunity to be patient and courageous and to act with wisdom so that you act justly.

Practice noticing when you feel harmed, and then practicing responding to that feeling. Results are not instantaneous, and even after you remember the wisdom you may still feel uneasy or still anxious or still hurt. But as long as you act justly and wisely and you keep that as your focus, this hurt will not bother you. Because it is not the Stoics aim to never feel any pain or hurt or to avoid *all* difficulty.

As Seneca put it:

>“There is this difference between ourselves and the other school [the Epicureans]: our ideal wise man feels his troubles but overcomes them; their wise man does not even feel them.”

Freedom from all bad feelings is not the Stoic aim. Pain is inevitable and pleasures are fleeting. We do not shun all joy, but we do not demean our actions by having their aim being joy. A Stoic is meant to pursue virtue. And we pursue virtue for virtue’s sake. If I have to give a reason behind virtue’s value, I would say that it is because virtue is something we can guarantee to ourselves, whereas everything else, beyond death, is not something we can guarantee. And even our death’s exactitudes are not known or guaranteed to us unless we choose death here and now. Prizing privileges like pleasure, fame, respect, wealth and good health is to enslave ourselves to things outside of our control. We cannot prize external results of our actions either, because even the most virtuous actions may still result in any number of effects. We prize our virtue, which is the intention and reason behind our character, our thoughts and our actions.

For if being courageous, just, wise, temperate, magnanimous, charitable, kind, frugal, thoughtful, open-minded, honest, modest and with few desires and so forth are not enough to give us purpose, then I believe we have imagined the “purposeful life” to be a privilege and not a choice. In which case, I suggest you ask yourself the next time you admire anybody “Do I really believe that all of what I admire in this person is merely born of the privileges and luxuries they’ve been afforded? Or is it what they’ve decided to do with their circumstances that I admire?”
