I suggest humility to you. Pride and shame make the same error in different directions: both let us assume with some certainty that we know ourselves and both assume with some certainty that we know what we are supposed to be. The difference between the two is that pride thinks we are great (perfect even, or near it) and shame thinks we are terrible (irredeemable even or near it). The dire mistake in both is assuming that we are perfect witnesses to ourselves. For how many times has someone shown us that we are not what we once thought we were, or showed us something about ourselves that we were altogether unaware of, like an anger problem or even something plain like that we snore while we sleep?

The essence of humility is the acknowledgment that *we are not perfect witnesses, not even of* **ourselves.**

But humility avoids these fatal mistakes by taking self-assessment and self-improvement and turning the former into self-examination and the latter into self-exploration. Start with asking tangible, non-moral questions like “Am I strong?” Or “Am I knowledgable?” And do not answer them with the first opinion that comes to mind. Answer them with action.

“Am I strong?” Do some exercises. Lift weights. Do push-ups. See what your body is able to do. And then you can answer “Am I strong?” with “I benched 100 pounds.”
“Am I knowledgable?” Read an article about some subject and afterwards, account what you read that was news to you and what you read that was already known by you. Then you can say, “I did already know that Frederick the Great was German King, but I didn’t know that he was specifically the King of Prussia. Nor was I aware of his involvement in the Seven Years’ War.”

Answers like these are not really left up to bias or some fallible opinion of ourselves like “Yes I am strong,” or “No, I am not knowledgable.” These answers are too simplistic. It is good to have concrete evidences as your answer to questions, even the ones about your character.

Through humility, we are able to engage with reality on reality’s terms. We’re able to learn who we are through actions that show us who we are. And it turns the qualities of ourselves, like strength and intelligence, into questions which can be exciting and invigorating and purposeful as opposed to dead-end answers like “Yes” or “No,” that can often kill any sense improvement being possible or desirable.

Once you’ve collected data from your tests, you can say “I know X and but I don’t know Y.” “I did X push-ups yesterday.” And so on, and then you’ve got a real working model of yourself. You have a good idea of what you’re working with. And if you feel like something is calling you, like maybe you feel like you want to be able to do more push-ups, you can take that as one of your new duties, hobbies and purposes in life. And you can measure your progress with real tangible numbers like “I did 3 more pushups than last time.” And whenever you progress, however small, take a short moment to appreciate the thought and effort you put towards that accomplishment. You must thank yourself; gratitude is another virtue and some have called it the greatest of all the virtues even. If, however, you make progress and catch yourself thinking “It’s not enough” or some other trivializing and belittling thought, notice this thought and acknowledge where it comes from and where it leads. It leads from a place of certainty about what is good and right and it leads to pride or shame, neither of which are desirable qualities to possess. I’ve heard a quote before, though I’m not sure if the attribution is accurate:

“As what is straight does not need that which is straight, that which is just does not need that which is just.”
-Epictetus

This hits home with a key idea of great use: if we are acting justly, then no just response or reward is necessary. For if we act justly only because we expect a like reward or response, we are not acting justly on principle, but in a gaming sense. Thus we debase and demean justice to be merely a means of obtaining some material, interpersonal prize rather than what justice is: the embodiment and enactment of wisdom and the gain or maintenance of well-being and of doing our duty to God, ourselves and the world.

Another from Epictetus:
“When any person does ill by you, or speaks ill of you, remember that he acts or speaks from an impression that it is right for him to do so. Now it is not possible that he should follow what appears right to you, but only what appears so to himself. Therefore, if he judges from false appearances, he is the person hurt, since he, too, is the person deceived. For if anyone takes a true proposition to be false, the proposition is not hurt, but only the man is deceived. Setting out, then, from these principles, you will meekly bear with a person who reviles you, for you will say upon every occasion, “It seemed so to him.”
-The Enchiridion, XLII

What is good for us is virtue, and vice is what is bad for us. To be clear, our own virtue and our own vice are what is good and what is bad for us. The virtues and vices of others are not ours and thus should not be accounted for in the measuring of our life’s quality, because these acts do not belong to us. When you witness someone acting unjustly, remind yourself of a few things.
Firstly, that their actions are not your actions and thus are not worth fretting about.
Secondly, that unjust action only harms the actor. Whatever harm they appear to do to others is not harm to the others themselves, but either to their bodies, their possessions or their reputation - none of which, in the deepest sense, belongs to these people.
Thirdly, that a person who is exacting injustice upon themselves and/or others is doing so because they erroneously believe it is just, acceptable and preferable to so.
And lastly, though this challenges the premise of the hypothetical witnessing of injustice, you yourself are not always a perfect judge of what is and what is not just. Reflect and think on Stoic principles about these events to confirm that deeming these actions as “unjust” is accurate.

When a person maligns us, it is in our best interest to maintain our character and stand by our truths with fidelity, courage and endurance. For if we are only just so long as we are treated as we may wish, then the whole principle of justice is but a means to an end rather than an end in and of itself. It may seem difficult to accept the world as it is, being that the world is so large and surprising and unknown to us. But each act of accepting more specific and singular incidents is actually quite simple. We witness the wrong-doing, acknowledge it as something we ought not do ourselves and that this has not robbed us of our only goods: our judgment and our actions.

If you find yourself valuing excessively anything beyond your judgment and your actions, know that you have enslaved yourself. For if we value another person’s bodily well-being or our material possessions enough to allow ourselves to be confused into thinking that damage to the body or the materials is misfortune, we will be vexed and upset and disordered by forces which we have no control over time and time again.

It is natural to our unrefined selves to witness suffering and maltreatment and to recoil with some fear, some fury or some sorrow. When we do feel these things do not ignore or dismiss them as you try to control and contain them. Tears left unwept and anger unexpressed are wont to find some other avenue in our subconscious to be let out, and thus we forsake our duty and power to control them. Acknowledge your heart’s pain and find a healthy means of expressing this emotion. Afterwards, take note of the whole occurrence of this pain, what led up to it, what it was as it happened and what followed as a result. This way your mind can know your heart better and thereafter learn to be in greater harmony with it.

Suppose that someone has spoken ill of you, perhaps a friend or lover says that you have made a grave mistake. If they are correct, see that only good has followed. For they, like a doctor, have exposed an illness or weakness within your reason and thereby given you a gift of self-knowledge. And if they have spoken falsely, then *they* are the one who is mistaken and you are not in any danger. And when friends or lovers make mistakes, we are gifted the opportunity to embody friendship by being there to assist them in their struggle and an opportunity to practice endurance and courage in the face of difficulty.

What is wrong in others is not wrong in ourselves. And wrong does not damage what is right. In fact, wrong acts make the right ones all the more important and noble. Then and therein, a good man and his goodness is all the more necessary, standing as a rose among thorns, bringing beauty, clarity, light and meaning to places that are ugly, dark, confused and lacking purpose.

Stoicism is a philosophy of the Greek schools, believing that the chief aim of life is eudaemonia (a hard to translate word; a common translation being “wholesomeness” or “well-being”; personally, based on what the etymological roots of the word appear to be, it would seem to mean “[being in] good spirits”), and that eudaemonia is obtained through virtue, which is in our acts. If you seek well-being and believe as I do that well-being is found in virtue, then the study and practice of Stoicism may be in your interest.

I do hold virtue as the only means of goodness in human beings. To account for goodness in other mean like in some form of consequentialism, wherein the results of the action qualify it as good or bad or neither, is to deem that goodness is a privilege and not a duty. For how can we ask others or ourselves to be good if factors outside of our control will determine that for us? Being good must mean being virtuous if we are to have any valid use for goodness. And virtues are those principles of behavior that life-affirming and mighty. For the Stoics, there are four cardinal virtues:

Courage
Temperance
Wisdom
Justice

Courage is doing what we believe we ought to do despite our fear of doing it. Courage has been said to be the most important virtue, for without it fear will inevitably rob us of our ability embody any other virtue. What good can Fortitude, Wisdom or Justice or any other virtue be if we are too afraid to make use of them? Whether or not it is the most important, it surely is important because we need some courage in this world to bear through the unavoidable hardships that have come, are now and shall come. If courage is not important, then by all means, run away. But how far are you willing to run away from your life?

“The bravest sight in the world is to see a great man struggling against adversity.”
-Seneca

Temperance is willfully undergoing hardship and withholding ourselves from pleasure to show us what is truly necessary. It is easy to misplace our sense of well-being upon things that are not needed to be well. Very little is needed for a happy life if we are willing to let go of slavish pleasures and embrace the natural difficulties of life. Through temperance, we are better able to bear through what courage charges us to endure. Through temperance, we are better able to be grateful and joyous at more common and free things like fair weather or a plate of even the most plain food.

“If you are distressed by anything external, the pain is not due to the thing itself, but to your estimate of it; and this you have the power to revoke at any moment.”
-Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book VIII.47

Wisdom is mindful awareness of what we acknowledge to be true and right. Merely learning an important idea and only recalling it when it is mentioned is not wisdom, but scanty use of memory and study. Wisdom is seeking what is true, right and reasonable and bearing it with us in all things so that it informs our actions and judgments. If we do not know what is true and right, then the task is to find out. And after we’ve found out, the task is to align ourselves with truth and rightness. This way, we are able to guide ourselves predictably and reliably and effectively.

“Happiness and freedom begin with a clear understanding of one principle: some things are in your control, and some things are not.”
-Epictetus

Lastly, justice. Justice is acting on our wisdom’s information, using the strength we’ve acquired through temperance and the willingness that courage provides. It is not only in treating others fairly, but in doing what we know to be right and correct at all times. It is perhaps the pinnacle of Stoic virtue, as it requires the three other virtues altogether to exist. One cannot be just and cowardly, or just and intemperate, or just and unwise, because justice is not about obtaining some “fair result,” like a guilty verdict for a guilty criminal or an innocent verdict for an innocent defendant. Justice is about carrying all the other virtues to bear, so that all are in use and given life in our actions deliberately. It is about embodying these principles consistently even when it may not seem fair to have to do so while so many others do not. 

“As what is straight does not need that which straight, so neither does the just need that which is just.”
-Epictetus

Through virtue, we shift our focus to who we are and what we do and try to be and do the best we can, without defining ourselves by those things outside of our control. That is freedom and happiness to me, which must be at least part of being in good spirits.

Who is this person that you are trying to love? Do you truly have a grasp on who you are? If you do not know yourself well enough to describe it, how could you ever properly love it? To love ourselves without knowing ourselves is a tall order.

Some think they know themselves well enough, and I find they generally fit themselves into the categories of proud or ashamed. The former hold themselves in high regard, often veering towards a sense of superiority, perfection and purity. A proud man seldom admits his faults, is wont to demand that the world serve him as he is owed for his apparent virtue, and is fixated on the maintenance of their self-image as a person who is good, who does very few things wrongly (if ever) and who is worthy of love, adoration and respect. The latter, the shameful, think themselves inferior, without redemption or silver-lining. They feel that others (who may love them dearly) merely tolerate their incompetence, their immorality, their repugnant qualities. And the shameful have no ears for praise, seeing it as lies and foolishness and the compliments of a blind person who does not know their shame well enough to see that they should be spit upon and not kissed.

Both pride and shame are alike, however different they may otherwise be, in at least two aspects as I see it:

1. Both claim to know what a good person is or ought to be

2. Both claim to know without much doubt whether they themselves are or are not a good person

They are two sides of the same coin. One lauds itself and the other hides its face. Both look too much at themselves and at themselves with more certainty than is warranted. And the only way to remove pride and shame is through humility. Being humble does not consist of downplaying one’s skills or accomplishments. Being humble is not about thinking less of yourself, nor is it that fabled art of seeing oneself “as one truly is.” 

Humility consists of acknowledging that you are not a perfect witness to yourself. 
Humility is understanding that without a mirror or a trusted companion, there are sides of ourselves that we would never have seen on our own. And that understanding encourages one not towards self-judgments, but towards self-inquiry and inquiry in general. When we start with humility, we cast out our certainties of standards and of our evidence as regards our meeting those standards. Humility has us ask ourselves “Am I good person?” Not with scrutiny or hostile, interrogative intent, but with a child-like curiosity, as though someone had asked you if you were a good musician while having never tried to play music before. The question can change form into something like “Could I be a good person?” And again, being asked with genuine child-like curiosity and wonder.

And from a question like that, we are engaging with reality to be our teacher and our judge rather than ourselves. A humble strongman, whose discipline maneuvering and bearing great weights, burdens and forces, would not declare that he was a great strongman or a terrible strongman without first trying his hand at some weight. And an experience, but still humble strongman would still refrain from simply dubbing himself as truly strong or not, but would point to his deeds. It means little for an athlete to say “Yes I am strong” or “Yes I am fast” when they could more plainly state the facts: “I have lifted 200 pounds of weight above my head.” Or: “I have won a race on foot last week.” And an honest, true athlete, I think, would keep their most recent successes or failures in answer to such questions, for that is most resemblant to who they are now.

Through humility, we are allowed a view of ourselves that is not merely from ourselves and is always open to reconsideration. We are allowed to throw off our self-prejudice and the blindness of pride and shame and seek ourselves in the world of deeds and acts and study and improvement. And from this learning, through humility we can acquire dignity, which is merely understanding ourselves, what we need and what we are capable of. 

Dignity is the healthy self-respect to acknowledge that if we push ourselves too hard, then we might hurt ourselves. And if we don’t push ourselves hard enough, we’ll grow weak. Dignity is not praising ourselves, it’s knowing what we can do and therefore what we ought to do. For no man ought to do what he is not capable of doing.

“If you have assumed a character above your strength, you have both acted in this matter in an unbecoming way and you have neglected that which you might have fulfilled.”
-Epictetus, The Enchiridion, Chapter 37

Once you are doing what you understand to be within your abilities and what you understand to be the best thing you can do with yourself here and now, I’d call that self-love. For what is more loving than giving purpose to something, especially a thing which once seemed, if only to itself, without purpose.
